title: What is a CGM?
summary: A continuous glucose monitor uses a small sensor under the skin to estimate glucose repeatedly.
why: A sequence of readings can show direction and timing that a single measurement misses.
how: The sensor measures glucose in interstitial fluid and sends estimates to a reader or phone.
example: A learner compares a lunch reading with the trace from the following two hours.
caution: Gaps, warm-up periods and sensor errors can interrupt readings. Keep the meter and backup plan recommended for your device.
question: Can the sensor give a diagnosis on its own?
answer: A CGM measures patterns. Diagnosis uses appropriate clinical testing.

title: Interstitial versus blood glucose
summary: A fingerstick samples capillary blood, while a CGM estimates glucose in fluid around cells.
why: The two readings can differ at the same moment without either instrument being broken.
how: Glucose moves between blood and tissue fluid. Differences can become more noticeable during rapid change.
example: After exercise a learner sees two different numbers within a few minutes and checks the device guidance.
caution: Follow the manufacturer’s confirmation instructions when symptoms and the display disagree.
question: Should both numbers always match exactly?
answer: No. They reflect different compartments and both measurements have uncertainty.

title: CGM lag and accuracy
summary: Lag describes a delay between a blood glucose change and the displayed sensor response.
why: It can complicate interpretation just after treating a low or during a rapid rise.
how: Movement between compartments and sensor processing both contribute. Pressure on some sensors can also distort readings.
example: Someone wakes on their sensor arm to an unexpected low and follows their device’s confirmation procedure.
caution: Do not assume that every unexpected low is pressure-related. Treat symptoms and follow your safety plan.
question: Can I correct lag by adding a fixed number?
answer: No. Direction, speed of change and sensor conditions vary.

title: Trend arrows
summary: Arrows summarise how quickly glucose has been moving over recent readings.
why: The same displayed value can accompany a rising, steady or falling trace.
how: Manufacturers use different windows and thresholds to translate recent movement into an arrow.
example: Two sample displays both show 120 mg/dL. One follows a flat stretch, the other a rapid descent.
caution: An arrow is not a guaranteed future glucose value or a standalone dosing instruction.
question: Do arrows have identical meanings across brands?
answer: Check the legend for your own model.

title: Time in Range (TIR)
summary: TIR is the proportion of monitored time within an agreed glucose band.
why: It adds context to an average by showing how much time was spent within the band.
how: For many nonpregnant adults, reports use 70–180 mg/dL. Targets and bands vary with circumstances, including pregnancy.
example: In an illustrative day with complete data, 18 hours in band corresponds to 75% TIR.
caution: Check sensor coverage and time below range alongside TIR. A percentage can hide when lows happen.
question: Can two people have the same TIR and different risks?
answer: Yes. Their remaining time may be spent at different extremes.

title: Time Below Range (TBR)
summary: TBR is the share of recorded time below a defined glucose boundary.
why: It helps identify exposure to lows, including overnight episodes a person might not feel.
how: Reports commonly distinguish time below 70 and below 54 mg/dL. A cumulative “below 70” figure includes “below 54”.
example: A report looks reassuring overall, yet its overnight segment repeatedly drops below the lower boundary.
caution: Check whether a report uses cumulative or separate bands before adding percentages.
question: Does TBR count the number of low events?
answer: No. It measures duration, so one long event can contribute more than several short ones.

title: Time Above Range (TAR)
summary: TAR describes how much monitored time lies above the selected upper boundary.
why: It helps focus a review on when high glucose persists.
how: A report can separate higher bands, often above 180 and above 250 mg/dL for nonpregnant adults.
example: A person sees most above-range time after dinner and brings several meal and timing notes to a review.
caution: TAR does not explain the cause. Review illness, meal timing, delivery and missing data.
question: Can one brief peak dominate the whole percentage?
answer: The metric weights time. Prolonged elevations contribute more.

title: Glucose Management Indicator (GMI)
summary: GMI converts mean sensor glucose to a percentage for discussion alongside laboratory HbA1c.
why: A discrepancy can prompt a closer look at the time window, sensor coverage and red blood cell factors.
how: The conversion is a population-based relationship. It does not measure haemoglobin in a blood sample.
example: A recent change in routine shifts two weeks of sensor readings before a longer-term laboratory result catches up.
caution: A GMI value cannot diagnose diabetes or replace the lab test.
question: Is a difference always a sensor fault?
answer: No. The measures cover different processes and often different periods.

title: Glucose variability and CV
summary: Variability describes how widely glucose moves around its average. Coefficient of variation (CV) expresses the spread relative to the mean.
why: A stable trace and a trace with large swings can have the same average.
how: CV is standard deviation divided by mean glucose, multiplied by 100. It summarises spread without identifying a time of day.
example: Two example weeks average the same glucose. Only one includes frequent low and high excursions.
caution: Sparse data can give misleading precision. Look at the trace and time below range as well.
question: Does CV tell me whether mornings are the problem?
answer: No. Use time-of-day plots for that question.

title: Ambulatory Glucose Profile (AGP)
summary: An AGP places readings from many days on one 24-hour clock.
why: It helps separate a recurring pattern from a single unusual day.
how: A central line gives the median at each time of day; shaded bands show how widely values vary across days.
example: A wide afternoon band prompts a learner to compare school days with weekends.
caution: The median is a summary, not a recording of any one day. Check individual traces and data coverage.
question: What does a wider band mean?
answer: Values at that time varied more between the contributing days.
takeaways: The centre line is a median

title: Fingerstick confirmation
summary: A fingerstick meter estimates glucose in a small blood sample.
why: It provides a backup during sensor warm-up, signal loss or disagreement with symptoms.
how: Clean, dry hands and correctly stored, compatible strips matter to the measurement.
example: A person with low symptoms but an unexpected sensor value uses their backup plan and meter.
caution: Do not delay emergency help for severe symptoms while troubleshooting a device.
question: Is calibration the same as confirmation?
answer: Confirmation checks a reading. Calibration changes how certain sensors calculate values; follow model instructions.

title: Automated insulin delivery (AID)
summary: AID links a compatible CGM, an algorithm and an insulin pump.
why: The system can adjust delivery between manual decisions.
how: Sensor values inform changes to pump delivery. Many systems still need meal input and cannot remove insulin already absorbed.
example: A learner traces how a sensor signal reaches the algorithm and then the pump.
caution: Maintain a failure and backup plan. An algorithm cannot detect every infusion or sensor problem.
question: Can a sensor alone deliver insulin?
answer: No. Delivery requires the pump and compatible control system.
takeaways: Know the sensor, controller and pump

title: Open-source diabetes technology
summary: Open-source diabetes projects publish software or designs that can be inspected by a community.
why: They can help people understand data flows and the responsibilities involved in running a system.
how: A display project and a closed-loop controller do different things. Read each project’s purpose, supported devices and regulatory context.
example: A reader compares the OpenAPS documentation with a commercial pump’s user manual.
caution: Public source code does not by itself establish regulatory approval, compatibility or clinical safety.
question: Does an open data dashboard automatically control a pump?
answer: No. Visualising data and controlling delivery are separate functions.

title: Nightscout
summary: Nightscout can make glucose data available through a privately managed website and API.
why: It enables remote viewing, but access settings determine who can see sensitive data.
how: A viewer requests readings from a configured server. Permissions, tokens and secure transport determine access.
example: A learner reads the Nightscout security guide before opening GlucoNest’s Devices & Data Sources screen.
caution: Never paste a private URL with a token into a public message. Use least-privilege access and review sharing settings.
question: Does this lesson connect to my server?
answer: No. Connection settings belong in Devices & Data Sources.

title: CGM alarms and alarm fatigue
summary: Alarm fatigue is the burden of frequent alerts competing for attention.
why: Repeated interruptions can disrupt sleep and make important alerts easier to miss.
how: Duplicate phone alerts, thresholds and signal-loss notifications can overlap. Each serves a different purpose.
example: A household lists which alerts woke each person and reviews them with the diabetes team.
caution: Do not silence safety-critical alarms without a safe alternative agreed with the team.
question: Can a shared-alert plan help?
answer: Agree who responds, when to check in and what to do if contact fails.

title: Sensor adhesion and skin
summary: Wear time and skin comfort depend on sensor placement, adhesive and the insertion site.
why: A lifting sensor or inflamed skin can affect both wear and confidence in readings.
how: Approved sites differ by model and age. Sweat, friction and reactions to adhesives can complicate wear.
example: Someone notes which patch caused irritation and discusses compatible alternatives with their clinic.
caution: Persistent redness, pain, warmth or broken skin needs assessment. Follow the device instructions for removal and replacement.
question: Can a sensor go anywhere comfortable?
answer: Use the insertion sites approved for that particular device.

title: Device compatibility and privacy
summary: Compatibility means the specific sensor, pump, phone and software versions can work together as intended.
why: A phone update or changed sharing permission can interrupt data or expose information.
how: A compatible radio connection alone does not establish compatibility for treatment decisions. Check manufacturer support lists.
example: Before changing phones, a user checks the exact operating system version and how to transfer alerts.
caution: Review data recipients and access tokens. Keep a backup way of checking glucose during a change.
question: Does sharing a graph require sharing an administrator password?
answer: Use the least privilege supported by the platform rather than giving full control.
